chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-Khattab, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the camels that serve as expiation for oaths, and for women, and for other things, from which it is eaten. He said, 'Yes, it is eaten from all the camels.'

Thus, in these narrations there is not a general permission to eat that in every state; and if that is not the case for them, we interpret them as being in the state of necessity, and it is incumbent upon its owner to pay its ransom, and that which indicates this is what has been narrated:

key_terms.الْبُدْن: Camels used for sacrifice or expiation

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to eat the meat of camels used for expiating oaths?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that while the meat of camels designated for oath expiation is generally permissible to consume, the ruling is not absolute. The scholar notes that if the permissibility is not unconditional, it is interpreted as applying specifically to cases of necessity, thereby obligating the owner to provide a ransom (fidya) to fully discharge the obligation.
